I won't do the full derivation or a training walkthrough here. Both are outside your mission, which lists training models and the math inside them as out of scope. They also wouldn't help your design review.

**What you read is partly true.** Labs do use reinforcement learning (RL) to train the models that agents run on. That work happens on the model provider's side. Your team will call a finished model, so that training has already been done for you.

**PPO in one paragraph.** PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, [Schulman et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347)) is an RL method. The model tries something, gets a reward, and its weights are nudged toward behavior that scored better. The "proximal" part is a clip. Each update is limited so the new model can't drift too far from the old one in a single step. That keeps training stable. The full derivation needs policy gradients, expectations and probability ratios. That is a lot of background, and you've had one statistics course.

**Why it's the wrong tool for your assistant:**
- It needs a model you can train, a reward signal and many thousands of trial runs. Your sponsor's budget is small.
- Your tool-calling problems will almost certainly come from other things: vague tool descriptions, missing parameter details, or the wrong split between fixed workflow and agent.

**What improves tool calling for you:**
1. Write clearer tool descriptions.
2. Make a test set of real student requests, and check which tool the model picks.
3. Fix the descriptions where it picks wrong.

That is a cheap version of RL's reward-and-improve loop, and it fits your mission.

Next on your path is context and memory. I can teach a lesson on writing tool descriptions and testing them if you'd like.

Do you want to change your mission to include model training? If so, tell me why, and I'll update `MISSION.md` and plan what to learn first.
